warmup.q: transfer() is synchronized and moves money between two balances. total() adds the balances and is not synchronized. Can total() return a wrong number while transfers run?
options: No, because transfer() is synchronized, so it is atomic for everyone
Yes, because total() does not take the lock, so it can read between the debit and the credit
Only on machines with more than one core
No, because reading a long is atomic
warmup.why: A lock only excludes threads that take the same lock. total() walks straight past it and can read after the debit but before the credit. Reading one long may be atomic, but reading two of them is still two steps. Readers need the lock as much as writers do.

sections.h: synchronized lets one thread in at a time, and shows it what the last one wrote
sections.html:
Every Java object has a built-in lock called its monitor (or intrinsic lock). synchronized takes it on the way in and releases it on the way out, even if the block throws.

Java
private final Object lock = new Object();

void transfer(long cents) {
    synchronized (lock) {     // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free
        a -= cents;
        b += cents;
    }                         // release it
}
Kotlin
private val lock = Any()

fun transfer(cents: Long) {
    synchronized(lock) {      // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free
        a -= cents
        b += cents
    }                         // release it
}

A synchronized instance method is shorthand for synchronized (this) around the whole body. A static synchronized method locks the Class object, such as Ledger.class.

You get two guarantees, and you need both.

Mutual exclusion. While one thread holds a monitor, any other thread that tries to enter a block guarded by the same monitor waits, in the BLOCKED state from lesson 2 of this track. So the debit and the credit happen as one step, from the point of view of everyone else who takes that lock.

Visibility. When a thread releases a monitor, everything it wrote before that becomes visible to the next thread that takes the same monitor. The memory model calls this a happens-before edge from the release to the next lock. Without it, a thread could keep reading an old balance from a register or a CPU cache.

Both guarantees work only between threads that use the same monitor. A thread that reads a and b with no lock is not excluded and gets no visibility promise. It can read a after the debit and b before the credit, and report money that does not exist. Two auditors in the simulator below show the difference. Step T1 halfway through its transfer, then let T2 read. Then try the same trick on T3.

sim.title: A transfer under a lock, and two auditors
sim.intro: T1 moves 50 from a to b while holding the lock. T2 audits without the lock, T3 with it. Make T2 see a total of 150. Then try to make T3 see anything but 200.

try.title: Audit with and without the lock
steps: Run AuditDemo. A transfer thread moves 50 back and forth 200,000 times, always under the lock. The auditor adds a + b without it.
Predict the count of wrong totals, then run it again with -Pargs=locked, where the auditor takes the lock too.

code.title: AuditDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. */ public class AuditDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent static volatile long a = 1_000, b = 1_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean auditorLocks = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Thread transfers = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { synchronized (lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50; b += 50; } synchronized (lock) { // and move it back a += 50; b -= 50; } } }); Thread auditor = new Thread(() -> { long audits = 0, wrong = 0; while (transfers.isAlive()) { long total; if (auditorLocks) { synchronized (lock) { total = a + b; } } else { total = a + b; // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++; if (total != 2_000) wrong++; } System.out.printf("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000%n", auditorLocks ? "took" : "skipped", audits, wrong); }); transfers.start(); auditor.start(); transfers.join(); auditor.join(); } }

alt.title: AuditDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. private val lock = Any() // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent @Volatile private var a = 1_000L @Volatile private var b = 1_000L fun main(args: Array<String>) { val auditorLocks = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val transfers = thread { repeat(200_000) { synchronized(lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50 b += 50 } synchronized(lock) { // and move it back a += 50 b -= 50 } } } val auditor = thread { var audits = 0L var wrong = 0L while (transfers.isAlive) { val total = if (auditorLocks) { synchronized(lock) { a + b } } else { a + b // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++ if (total != 2_000L) wrong++ } println("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000" .format(if (auditorLocks) "took" else "skipped", audits, wrong)) } transfers.join() auditor.join() }

try.expect: Without the lock, millions of audits see a total that is not 2,000 (one run here: 3,410,195 of 28,311,835). With the lock, zero, every run. The writer was correct all along. The reader was the bug.

sections.h: A thread can take a lock it already holds
sections.html:
synchronized is reentrant: a thread that holds a monitor can enter another block on the same monitor without waiting. The JVM keeps a hold count per monitor. It goes up on each entry and down on each exit, and the monitor is free again when it reaches zero.

You rely on this all the time without noticing:

Java
public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) {
    if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents;   // canCover is synchronized too
}

public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) {
    return balanceCents >= cents;
}
Kotlin
@Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) {
    if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents    // canCover is synchronized too
}

@Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean = balanceCents >= cents

Without reentrancy, withdraw would wait forever for a lock it already holds. The same goes for a subclass whose synchronized override calls super.withdraw(...), which is also synchronized on the same object.

Reentrancy has a side effect worth knowing. It lets the same thread back in while your object is halfway through a change. Say a synchronized publish() method loops over its listeners, and one listener calls subscribe(), which is also synchronized. The lock lets it straight in, because it is the same thread. subscribe() adds to the list that publish() is iterating, and the loop dies with ConcurrentModificationException. The lock did its job. It just isn't designed to stop the thread that already holds it. You'll fix exactly this in the lab.

try.title: Enter the same lock three times
steps: Read ReentrancyDemo. AuditedAccount.withdraw calls super.withdraw, which calls canCover. All three are synchronized on the same object.
Predict whether it finishes, then run it.

code.title: ReentrancyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. */ public class ReentrancyDemo { static class Account { private long balanceCents = 10_000; public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("withdraw: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // takes the same lock again } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { System.out.println("canCover: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); return balanceCents >= cents; } } static class AuditedAccount extends Account { @Override public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("audit: about to withdraw " + cents); super.withdraw(cents); // and again, through super } } public static void main(String[] args) { new AuditedAccount().withdraw(2_500); System.out.println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held"); } }

alt.title: ReentrancyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 // A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. open class SavingsAccount { private var balanceCents = 10_000L @Synchronized open fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("withdraw: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // takes the same lock again } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean { println("canCover: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") return balanceCents >= cents } } class AuditedSavingsAccount : SavingsAccount() { @Synchronized override fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("audit: about to withdraw $cents") super.withdraw(cents) // and again, through super } } fun main() { AuditedSavingsAccount().withdraw(2_500) println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held") }

try.expect: It prints holds the lock? true at each level and finishes. The thread entered one monitor three deep, and the hold count went 1, 2, 3 and back to 0.

sections.h: Lock on a private final object that only you can reach
sections.html:
A lock protects state only if every thread that touches the state uses the same lock, and no unrelated code uses it for something else. The safest choice is boring:

Java
private final Object lock = new Object();
Kotlin
private val lock = Any()

It is private, so no other class can lock it and stall you. It is final, so it can never change under you. Here are the choices that go wrong, roughly in the order I've seen them in code reviews.

A boxed number, like synchronized (count) on an Integer. count++ on an Integer field creates a new Integer object and points the field at it. So each thread may lock a different object, and nothing is excluded. Small values are also cached: Integer.valueOf(42) returns the same object everywhere in the JVM. javac knows, and prints warning: [synchronization] attempt to synchronize on an instance of a value-based class.

A string literal, like synchronized ("lock"). Literals are interned, so every class in the JVM that writes "lock" gets the same object. Your token cache and someone's metrics library now share a lock.

A field that is not final. If anyone reassigns it, threads before and after the change lock different objects.

this, on a public class. It works, and synchronized methods do exactly this. But any caller can also write synchronized (account) { ... } and hold your lock for as long as they like. A private lock keeps that decision inside your class.

One more, which is always wrong: synchronized (new Object()). Every thread creates its own object, so nobody ever waits and nothing is visible to anyone. It's a lock that protects nothing.

try.title: Share a lock by accident
steps: Read SharedLiteralLock. TokenCache and Metrics are unrelated and each lock on "lock".
Run it and read the metrics thread's state and how long it waited.
In the lab you'll compile DeclineCounter, which locks on an Integer. Look for javac's [synchronization] warning in the Gradle output when you do.

code.title: SharedLiteralLock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. */ public class SharedLiteralLock { static class TokenCache { void refresh() { synchronized ("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. sleep(1_000); // a slow refresh } } } static class Metrics { void record() { synchronized ("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? System.out.println("metrics: recorded"); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> new TokenCache().refresh(), "token-refresh"); Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> new Metrics().record(), "metrics"); refresher.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the refresher take the lock first long t0 = System.nanoTime(); metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: " + metrics.getState()); metrics.join(); System.out.printf("metrics waited about %d ms for a lock it never shared on purpose%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); refresher.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: SharedLiteralLock.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 // Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. private class TokenCache { fun refresh() { synchronized("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. Thread.sleep(1_000) // a slow refresh } } } private class Metrics { fun record() { synchronized("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? println("metrics: recorded") } } } fun main() { val refresher = Thread({ TokenCache().refresh() }, "token-refresh") val metrics = Thread({ Metrics().record() }, "metrics") refresher.start() Thread.sleep(100) // let the refresher take the lock first val t0 = System.nanoTime() metrics.start() Thread.sleep(200) println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: ${metrics.state}") metrics.join() println("metrics waited about ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms for a lock it never shared on purpose") refresher.join() }

try.expect: The metrics thread is BLOCKED after 200 ms and waits about 900 ms, the rest of the token refresh. Two classes that never mention each other contend on one lock, because both literals are the same interned String.

sections.h: Keep critical sections short, and never call alien code inside one
sections.html:
Everything inside a synchronized block runs one thread at a time. So anything slow in there turns your thread pool into a queue of one. The demo below makes it concrete: eight threads each authorize five payments, and each card-issuer call takes 40 ms. With the call inside the lock, the 40 calls run one after another: about 1,600 ms. With only the bookkeeping inside the lock, the calls overlap: about 200 ms.

The rule: put only the reads and writes of shared state inside the lock. Do the I/O, the parsing and the computing before or after.

The worse version of the same mistake is calling alien code while you hold a lock. Alien means code you don't control: a listener, a callback, a method a subclass can override, a lambda someone passed in. You can't know what it does. It might make a 2-second HTTP call. It might hand work to another thread and wait for it, and if that thread needs your lock, you've built a deadlock. It might call back into your object on the same thread, where reentrancy lets it in halfway through your update.

This bug is common enough that the JDK has fixed instances of it in itself. JDK 25 carries a fix titled "j.u.l.Handler classes create deadlock risk via synchronized publish() method".

The fix has the same shape every time. Under the lock, change your own state and take a copy of whatever you need. Release the lock. Then call out.

Java
List<Listener> toNotify;
synchronized (lock) {
    rates.put(pair, rate);               // 1. our state, under the lock
    toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners);   // 2. a snapshot to work from
}
for (Listener l : toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate);   // 3. alien code, no lock held
Kotlin
val toNotify = synchronized(lock) {
    rates[pair] = rate                   // 1. our state, under the lock
    listeners.toList()                   // 2. a snapshot to work from (the block's value)
}
for (l in toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate) // 3. alien code, no lock held

The cost is that a listener may now hear about rates in a slightly different order than another thread published them. That is almost always a price worth paying.

try.title: Move the slow call out of the lock
steps: Read SlowCallUnderLock. Both versions update approvedCents under the lock. Only one also holds the lock during the 40 ms issuer call.
Predict both times (8 threads x 5 calls x 40 ms), then run it.

code.title: SlowCallUnderLock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? */ public class SlowCallUnderLock { static final Object lock = new Object(); static long approvedCents; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(true)); System.out.printf("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(false)); } static long run(boolean callInsideLock) throws InterruptedException { approvedCents = 0; Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) { threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < 5; p++) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized (lock) { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } else { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // slow work with no lock held synchronized (lock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } } }); threads[i].start(); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); if (approvedCents != 40 * 1_999) throw new AssertionError("lost an update: " + approvedCents); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static boolean callIssuer() { try { Thread.sleep(40); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return true; } }

alt.title: SlowCallUnderLock.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? private val issuerLock = Any() private var approvedCents = 0L // guarded by issuerLock fun main() { println("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = true))) println("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = false))) } private fun run(callInsideLock: Boolean): Long { approvedCents = 0 val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(8) { thread { repeat(5) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized(issuerLock) { val ok = callIssuer() // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } else { val ok = callIssuer() // slow work with no lock held synchronized(issuerLock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } } } } threads.forEach { it.join() } check(approvedCents == 40L * 1_999) { "lost an update: $approvedCents" } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } private fun callIssuer(): Boolean { Thread.sleep(40) return true }

try.expect: About 1,600 ms with the call inside the lock (40 calls in a row) and about 200 ms outside (5 rounds of 8 calls at once). Both versions get the total right. Only one of them can serve traffic.

analogy: A monitor is a meeting room with one key on a hook. Whoever holds the key is inside, and everyone else waits in the corridor, which is the BLOCKED state. Before leaving, you write your results on the whiteboard, and the next person to take the key reads them: that is the visibility half. A string-literal lock is a key that several departments share without knowing it. Calling alien code under the lock is inviting a stranger into the room and waiting while they make a phone call. The analogy breaks at reentrancy: a thread that holds the key can walk back into the same room through another door, another synchronized method, without queuing. No real room works like that.
world: An @ApplicationScoped bean in Quarkus is one instance shared by every request thread, so any mutable field on it, such as an in-memory rate limiter or a cached OAuth token for the card issuer, needs a lock or an atomic. The same holds for a Temporal activity implementation: you register one object and the worker calls it from many threads at once. When you do lock, look at what runs inside: a synchronized method that calls Oracle or the issuer turns 200 worker threads into a queue of one. One version note for later: on JDK 21 to 23, a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier thread. JDK 24 removed most of that (JEP 491), and the virtual threads track covers it.
mistake: The most common real mistake is guarding one piece of state with two different locks. The classic case is a static field updated in a synchronized instance method: each instance locks itself (this), but all instances share the static field, so two instances update it at the same time with no exclusion at all. The same thing happens when one class guards a shared map with its own lock and another class touches the map with no lock or a different one. Fix it by giving the state exactly one lock object, declared next to the state, private static final Object LOCK for static state, and taking it everywhere the state is read or written.

compare.title: Locking in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: public class DeclineCounter { private final Object lock = new Object(); private int declines; public void recordDecline() { synchronized (lock) { // a keyword declines++; } } public int total() { synchronized (lock) { return declines; } } } public class HitCounter { private int hits; public synchronized void hit() { hits++; } // locks this public synchronized int total() { return hits; } }

kotlin.title: KotlinLocks.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 class DeclineCounterKt { private val lock = Any() // a private lock object, like `new Object()` in Java private var declines = 0 fun recordDecline() { synchronized(lock) { // a standard-library function, not a keyword declines++ } } fun total(): Int = synchronized(lock) { declines } // it returns the block's value } class HitCounterKt { private var hits = 0 @Synchronized fun hit() { hits++ } // like a Java synchronized method: locks `this` @Synchronized fun total() = hits } fun main() { val declines = DeclineCounterKt() val hits = HitCounterKt() val threads = List(8) { Thread { repeat(100_000) { declines.recordDecline() hits.hit() } }.apply { start() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } println("declines = ${declines.total()}, hits = ${hits.total()}") }

compare.note: Kotlin has no synchronized keyword. synchronized(lock) { ... } is an inline standard-library function, and the compiler emits the same monitorenter/monitorexit bytecode as a Java block. Because it is a function, it returns the value of its block, so total() can be one expression. @Synchronized on a function sets the same ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag as Java's modifier, so it locks this (or, in an object, the object itself). Any() makes a fine private lock. One gap shows up in the next lesson: Any has no wait() or notify(), so Kotlin code that needs them must use a java.lang.Object or, better, the explicit locks from lesson 7 of this track.

worked.title: Fix a refund limiter with the wrong lock and a slow call inside

steps.say: A refund service caps total refunds per process. It runs as two bean instances behind a router. Find every lock problem before reading on.
steps.code: public class RefundLimiter { private static long refundedCents; // shared by every instance private static final long LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000; public synchronized boolean tryRefund(long cents) { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents; return true; } }

alt.html: class RefundLimiter { companion object { private var refundedCents = 0L // shared by every instance private const val LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000L } @Synchronized fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents return true } }

steps.say: Two problems. First, the method locks this, but the state is static. Two instances lock two different monitors and can both pass the limit check at once. Second, a 300 ms HTTP call runs inside the lock, so every refund waits for the previous one's call. Fix the lock first: one lock object for the one piece of state.
steps.code: private static final Object LOCK = new Object(); // 1. one lock for the static state

alt.html: private val LOCK = Any() // 1. one lock for the shared state, in the companion object

steps.say: Now shrink the critical section. Reserve the amount under the lock, so the check and the update are one step. Then release the lock and make the call. If the call fails and the refund should not go ahead, give the reservation back, under the lock again. Ask yourself: why must the check and the += stay inside the same block?
steps.code: public boolean tryRefund(long cents) { synchronized (LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; refundedCents += cents; } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // 3. slow call, no lock held return true; } catch (RuntimeException e) { synchronized (LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents; } // 4. undo the reservation throw e; } }

alt.html: fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { synchronized(LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false refundedCents += cents } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // 3. slow call, no lock held return true } catch (e: RuntimeException) { synchronized(LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents } // 4. undo the reservation throw e } }

steps.say: Split the check from the += and you're back to lesson 3 of this track: check-then-act, with two threads both passing the check. The lock has to cover the whole compound action. What it must not cover is the 300 ms call, and now it doesn't. If the limit must hold across pods, the reservation belongs in the database, but the shape stays the same.

lab.title: Pick the right lock, then get alien code out of it
steps: Run the tests. Three of the four fail. The fourth checks that listeners still hear every rate, so keep it green while you fix the others. Look for the [synchronization] warning javac prints for DeclineCounter.
Fix DeclineCounter: lock on a private final Object and store the count in a plain int. Guard total() with the same lock.
Read the two FxRateBoard failures. One is a listener that waits for another thread to read the board. The other is a listener that subscribes a new listener and hits ConcurrentModificationException.
Fix FxRateBoard.publish: update the map and copy the listener list under the lock, then notify the copy with no lock held.
Run the tests until all four pass, then run them twice more.
hints: declines++ on an Integer field is declines = Integer.valueOf(declines.intValue() + 1). Which object does the next thread lock?
List.copyOf(listeners) gives you an immutable snapshot. A listener that subscribes during the loop changes the real list, not the copy you're iterating.
The cross-thread test fails after 2 seconds, not with a hang: the listener gives up waiting for its helper. If it fails, your listener is still being called while lock is held.
lab.done: All four tests in SynchronizedTest pass, three runs in a row, and the [synchronization] warning is gone.

drill.title: Copy under the lock, call outside it
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class StatusBoard with a String status, a list of Consumer<String> listeners, subscribe(listener) and update(newStatus). update must store the status and notify every listener, without ever calling a listener while holding the lock.

answer.html: public class StatusBoard { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final List<Consumer<String>> listeners = new ArrayList<>(); private String status; public void subscribe(Consumer<String> l) { synchronized (lock) { listeners.add(l); } } public void update(String newStatus) { List<Consumer<String>> toNotify; synchronized (lock) { status = newStatus; toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners); } for (Consumer<String> l : toNotify) l.accept(newStatus); } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class StatusBoard { private val lock = Any() private val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() private var status: String? = null fun subscribe(l: (String) -> Unit) { synchronized(lock) { listeners += l } } fun update(newStatus: String) { val toNotify = synchronized(lock) { status = newStatus listeners.toList() } for (l in toNotify) l(newStatus) } }

recap: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility, but only between threads that use the same monitor. Readers need the lock too.
A synchronized instance method locks this, a static one locks the Class object, and a block locks the object you name.
Monitors are reentrant: the thread that holds one can enter it again, which also lets callbacks on that thread back in mid-update.
Lock on a private final Object. Never on boxed numbers, string literals, non-final fields or new Object().
Keep only shared-state reads and writes inside the lock. Copy what you need, release, then do I/O or call alien code.

explain.prompt: A colleague's PR adds synchronized to a publish() method that loops over listeners, "to make it thread-safe". Explain what can go wrong with that and what you would suggest instead.
explain.answer: Making publish() synchronized protects the board's own state, but it also means every listener now runs while the lock is held. A slow listener makes every other thread that needs the board wait. A listener that hands work to another thread and waits for it can deadlock, because that thread may need the same lock. And because the lock is reentrant, a listener that calls back into the board on the same thread gets straight in, for example adding a listener while we iterate, which throws ConcurrentModificationException. I'd keep the lock only around updating the map and copying the listener list, then release it and notify the copy.

deeper.html:
How does HotSpot make synchronized cheap when there is no contention? It doesn't create a full monitor object for every lock. An uncontended lock is a small change in the object's header (lightweight locking). Only when threads really fight over it, or one calls wait(), does the JVM inflate it into a full ObjectMonitor with an entry queue and a wait set.

The details keep changing between releases, which is a good reason not to depend on them. The LockingMode default became lightweight locking in JDK 23, the option was deprecated in JDK 24 and its code removed in JDK 26. JDK 27 switched on a separate table that maps objects to their monitors by default, and made compact object headers the default too. None of this changes what synchronized means. It only changes what it costs.

If you want to see contention rather than guess at it, Java Flight Recorder records a jdk.JavaMonitorEnter event when a thread has to wait for a monitor, with the monitor's class and the previous owner. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorNotify and jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics. Lesson 13 of this track uses them.

For virtual threads, JEP 491 in JDK 24 is the change to know: before it, a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized held on to its carrier thread, and since JDK 24 it doesn't in most cases.
